title: Artificial reproduction
summary:
Artificial reproduction is the re-creation of life brought about by means other than natural ones. It is new life built by human plans and projects. Examples include artificial selection, artificial insemination, in vitro fertilization, artificial womb, artificial cloning, and kinematic replication.

Humans have aspired to create life since immemorial times. Most theologies and religions have conceived this possibility as exclusive of deities. Although ancient Greek philosophy raised the concept that man could imitate the creative capacity of nature, classic Greeks thought that if possible, human beings would reproduce things as nature does. Aristotle wrote that if nature made tables, it would make them just as men do. Correspondingly, Descartes envisioned the human body, and nature, as a machine.

Because Biosemiotics does not focus on the function of life but on its meaning, it has a better understanding of the artificial than classic biology. Biology addresses reproduction in terms of growth and cellular division, but the science of artificial reproduction is not restricted by the mirroring of these natural processes and is actually transcending the natural forms and rules of reproduction. For example, xenobots have redefined the classical conception of reproduction. Although xenobots are made of eukaryotic cells, they do not reproduce by mitosis but rather by kinematic replication. Such constructive replication does not involve growing but rather building.

Related topics include assisted reproductive technology (ART), whose purpose is to assist the development of a human embryo commonly because of fertility limitations; cloning, the cellular reproductive process where genetically identical organisms are created by artificial means including editing the genetic code and somatic cell nuclear transfer; and artificial wombs, devices that allow for ectogenesis or extracorporeal pregnancy by growing an embryonic form outside the body of an organism.
